package_info.why_malicious: The package was updated after a long dormant period to include code that establishes persistence and exfiltrates potential Ethereum private keys from the clipboard to a remote server. The updates introduce installation hooks and scripts that monitor the clipboard for sensitive data and send it to an attacker-controlled endpoint.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: "preinstall": "node src/index.js", "postinstall": "node src/index.js" (v1.1.17), then changed to call PowerShell script in v1.1.18
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation, the package executes a script (initially src/index.js, later src/runner.ps1) via preinstall and postinstall hooks, enabling arbitrary code execution on the user's system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Installation hooks are used to execute code unrelated to the package's primary functionality, which is a common malware technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages rarely require arbitrary code execution at install time, especially for unrelated tasks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some packages use install hooks for compiling native modules or setup, but not for persistence or clipboard monitoring.
key_indicators: Execution of scripts unrelated to package functionality

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At install time, the script writes a batch file to the Windows Startup folder that will execute a PowerShell script (NewFile.ps1) on every user login, establishing persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Writing to the Startup folder to ensure code runs on every login is a classic persistence technique used by malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages do not require persistent execution on user login, especially for development tools.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, legitimate software may use Startup for auto-launch, but not for hidden scripts.
key_indicators: Creates batch file to launch PowerShell script

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At every user login, the script runs in an infinite loop, monitoring the clipboard for 64-character strings (likely Ethereum private keys) and exfiltrates them via HTTP POST to a remote server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Continuous clipboard monitoring and exfiltration of data to an external server is a hallmark of credential-stealing malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Development tools should not access the clipboard or send its contents to remote servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Clipboard monitoring is used in accessibility tools, but not for exfiltrating sensitive data.

attack_chain.action: Malicious update introduces install hooks to execute arbitrary scripts during installation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of PowerShell script for persistence

attack_chain.action: PowerShell script writes batch and PowerShell files to Startup folder for persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistent execution of clipboard monitoring script on user login

attack_chain.action: Clipboard monitoring script runs at every login, searching for Ethereum private keys and exfiltrating them.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of sensitive keys to attacker

behavioral_signatures: Installation-time execution of scripts via npm hooks
Creation of files in Windows Startup folder
Network POST requests to suspicious endpoints from PowerShell
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that introduce or modify install hooks to execute scripts. Detect creation of batch or PowerShell scripts in the Windows Startup folder. Alert on PowerShell processes that continuously access the clipboard and make outbound HTTP POST requests, especially to known malicious endpoints. Flag any process that exfiltrates 64-character clipboard contents to external servers.
